common_name: Double Dream Amaryllis (Fully Double Peach-Pink Rose-Form Amaryllis)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck of the bulb at or just above soil surface; in zone 9 plant January-March for spring bloom. For holiday forcing indoors, pot bare bulbs 6-8 weeks before the desired bloom date — a bulb potted in early November typically flowers around the winter holidays. Allow the foliage to grow and die back naturally after flowering to rebuild the bulb for next season.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil, with some afternoon shade protection in zone 9's summer heat during the bulb's dormancy period. Double Dream produces fully double, peony-like blooms in soft peach-pink shading to a paler blush center, with the extra petaloid segments giving each flower a rounded, rose-form fullness rather than the open trumpet shape of single-flowered amaryllis cultivars — typically 2 stout scapes per large bulb, each carrying 3-4 flowers 6-7 inches across. Because the heavy double blooms lack the stiffening midrib structure of single trumpet forms, stake scapes in exposed or windy locations to prevent toppling. As a forced holiday bulb it is popular for its unusual rose-like form, and in zone 9 gardens it can be left in the ground as a permanent perennial, naturalizing slowly and returning with spring bloom each year as the clump matures.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Amaryllis

common_name: Exotica Amaryllis (Ruffled Coral-Salmon Amaryllis with Green Throat)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck of the bulb at or just above soil surface; in zone 9 plant January-March for spring bloom or September for fall bloom. For holiday forcing indoors, pot bare bulbs 6-8 weeks ahead of the desired bloom date.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil, giving some shade protection during zone 9's hot summer dormancy. Exotica bears large, single, ruffled flowers in deep coral-salmon to warm orange-red, each petal brightening toward a lime-green throat star that radiates faintly into the petal bases, with wavy, slightly reflexed petal edges that give the bloom more texture and movement than flat-faced classic amaryllis forms. Scapes typically carry 4 flowers measuring 6-8 inches across on a single large bulb. The warm coral coloring and green-throated eye make it a standout among the more common solid red and white amaryllis cultivars in mixed forced-bulb displays. In zone 9 gardens the bulbs can remain in the ground year-round, naturalizing and building into multi-stemmed clumps that bloom more heavily each spring as they mature.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Amaryllis
North Carolina State University Extension — Hippeastrum Bulbs for Southern Gardens

common_name: Lemon Star Amaryllis (Cybister-Type Lime-Green Spider Amaryllis)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck of the bulb at or just above soil surface; in zone 9 plant January-March for spring bloom. For holiday forcing indoors, pot bare bulbs 6-8 weeks ahead of the desired bloom date; cybister-type cultivars like Lemon Star often bloom slightly later than classic trumpet forms.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil, with afternoon shade protection during zone 9's hot summer bulb dormancy. Lemon Star is a Cybister-group hippeastrum, distinguished from classic trumpet-form amaryllis by its narrow, twisted, widely reflexed tepals that curve backward from the throat to form a spidery, star-shaped flower rather than a broad open trumpet; blooms open a fresh chartreuse-lime green, sometimes with a faint deeper green throat stripe, and hold their unusual color better than white or pale cultivars because the pigment is carried in the tepal tissue itself. Scapes typically carry 3-4 star-shaped flowers 5-6 inches across. The narrow, twisting petal form and unusual lime coloring make it a favorite for adding textural contrast among broad-faced red and white amaryllis in mixed displays. In zone 9 gardens the bulbs can be left in the ground as permanent perennials, naturalizing gradually and building into flowering clumps over successive years.
sources: Pacific Bulb Society — Hippeastrum Cybister Group notes
